messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Counselor
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 74

Mark, a 55-year-old Caucasian counselor, has been navigating the aftermath of a traumatic event that occurred three years ago. He remains single and maintains an active role in his community through his work as a counselor. Mark's life took a drastic turn when he was caught in the midst of a devastating factory explosion in his hometown. The blast left numerous people injured or worse, and Mark himself barely escaped with his life. On that fateful day, Mark had stopped by the factory to pick up some supplies for an upcoming community event he was organizing. Suddenly, there was a deafening roar as the building erupted into flames. Mark remembers being jolted from his car, the ground shaking beneath him, and feeling disoriented as debris rained down around him. He escaped through a narrow alleyway, but the images of the burning factory and the sounds of people screaming have haunted him ever since. In the days following the explosion, Mark found it difficult to shake off the sense of panic and fear that had gripped him during the event. Night after night, he would wake up in a cold sweat, replaying the scene over and over again in his mind. He began experiencing intense flashbacks whenever he heard loud noises or saw flames on TV. His heart would race, and he felt as though he were reliving that terrible day all over again. Mark’s work as a counselor took a toll; he found it increasingly difficult to help others when he himself was struggling with his own trauma. He noticed that clients who had experienced their own traumas triggered intense emotional reactions in him, making it hard for him to remain objective and supportive. As a result, Mark began avoiding these kinds of cases altogether, which significantly impacted his job performance. Socially, Mark has become more withdrawn since the explosion. He used to be an active participant in community events and social gatherings but now finds himself canceling plans or staying quiet during group conversations. The fear that something like the factory blast could happen again is ever-present, making him feel unsafe even in familiar settings. Mark’s relationships have suffered as a result of his PTSD symptoms. Friends often describe him as distant and emotionally unavailable. They worry about him but struggle to understand why he has pulled away so much since the incident. Mark feels guilty for pushing people away yet finds it nearly impossible to let anyone close enough to see how deeply troubled he truly is. On top of everything else, Mark experiences severe anxiety when driving past the site where the explosion occurred. The sight of the now-closed factory sends waves of distress through him, causing his hands to tremble and his mind to race with worst-case scenarios. He avoids that route whenever possible, rerouting his commute even though it adds an hour to each trip. Despite his efforts to manage these symptoms on his own, Mark has found himself increasingly reliant on alcohol to help him sleep at night. While the drinks provide temporary relief from nightmares and intrusive thoughts, they leave him feeling more exhausted and depressed in the morning. This cycle of drinking and waking up with lingering dread has only worsened over time. As a counselor, Mark is acutely aware that his PTSD is affecting not just himself but also those around him. He recognizes that he needs help to process what happened and find healthier ways to cope, yet the thought of seeking therapy feels overwhelming given how much control he usually maintains in his life and work. Nevertheless, there’s an underlying hope that perhaps by sharing his story with someone new, Mark can start making sense of the chaos within him.
